unit.title: If every step was fair, is the result fair?
unit.needIt: Some people end up with far more than others. Whether that is unjust depends on whether you judge the final shares or how they came about.
unit.why: Nozick tells a story about a fair starting point where everyone has an equal amount of money. Then, people freely choose to give their money to a famous basketball player. Even though the result is very unequal, Nozick argues it is still just because every choice was free and honest.
unit.outcome: Evaluate whether a social outcome is fair based on the process used to reach it.
unit.reachesYou: You see this when you wonder why some people are rich while others are poor. It also shows up when you think about whether it is fair for a company to pay its workers a lot of money.
unit.do: Think about a time you shared something. Ask yourself if it felt fair because of the result or because of how you decided to share it.

quiz.q: What is the core of Nozick's picture?
quiz.why: Nozick sees the core of inviolability as a notion of rights.
quiz.quote: He sees it as lying in a notion of rights.

quiz.q: What is the most extensive state Nozick can justify?
quiz.why: Nozick argues that the minimal state is the most extensive state that can be justified.
quiz.quote: And goes on to say that the minimal state limited to the narrow functions of protection against force, theft, fraud, the enforcement of contracts, and so on, is the most extensive state that can be justified.

quiz.q: What is the core of Rawls' picture?
quiz.why: The lecture states that Rawls' picture lies in a notion of justice.
quiz.quote: Perhaps because at the core of Rawls' picture lies a notion of justice, whereas at the core of Nozick's picture lies a notion of rights.

quiz.q: What does Nozick say matters most in justice in holdings?
quiz.why: Nozick stresses that the process by which one comes to possess an object is what matters.
quiz.quote: Nozick stresses that when you make use of the principles that he's articulated here, what matters is the process, not the outcome.

quiz.why: Historical principles tell us that whether a distribution is just depends on how it came about.
quiz.quote: He distinguishes between principles that are historical, that is, that tell us that whether a distribution is just depends upon how it came about.

quiz.q: What is the normative claim of the Wilt Chamberlain example?
quiz.why: Nozick argues that if people freely transfer resources, no injustice has occurred.
quiz.quote: And the normative claim is that in so doing, no injustice has occurred.

partials: Patterns can be upset by liberty.
crystal.key: Justice is a historical process of free choices, not a fixed pattern of results.

decoys.text: Justice is about the final distribution of wealth.
decoys.why: Nozick argues that end-result principles are not the way to determine justice.

decoys.text: The state should redistribute wealth to keep patterns fair.
decoys.why: Nozick argues that maintaining a pattern requires interfering with people's liberty.

crystal.aha: If the process of acquisition and transfer is just, the resulting distribution is just regardless of the pattern.

actors.label: No one was forced. Is it unfair?

beats.say: Everyone starts with the same ten coins.
Each freely drops one in a player's hat.
Now the player has far more than anyone.
For Nozick justice is in how holdings came about, not the shares.
